summary.en: Laura describes quietly shipping a high-impact onboarding change late at night and discovering it lifted conversion by about 5% with no personalization. She emphasizes the value of asking forgiveness rather than permission for small, reversible experiments. The episode is full of pragmatic growth-testing wisdom from a seasoned operator.

turns.en: Career growth is definitely not a straight lineup, but there's definitely some frameworks and methods that have worked really well for me. And I think to dive into it, it's first good to just talk about the one that I most typically see people use to try to grow their career and why that can be a little problematic, which is that I see most people try to work really hard the job that they have within the role that they have at a company. Do whatever you can to grow there, show your manager all these things. I see people keep spreadsheets, it wins. So it can come up with performance reviews. Maybe you try to get better advocating for yourself, maybe try to get peers to notice or your manager's peers. And that's all good. It's all stuff. (00:06:52): But the problem with it is that you're limited to what your manager's ability is to advocate for you, to promote you. And you're also limited by the explicit trajectory of your role at that company and where the there's room for that or not at the company. And then often that perception can sometimes be a little bit in contrast to what your perception is. And also other things that happen, your manager leaves and then you have to restart with someone else. So the method that I use tries to take that power back a little bit. And something that I learned really early on in my career, I was very lucky to learn by accident, was at a company called Bandwidth, which is my first real job. And Bandwidth is now a public company and they've done all kinds of crazy amazing things. (00:07:38): But I joined when it was just 50 people and I actually joined in sales and I was just hungry to make it succeed and grow and bright eyes and everything, first real job. But I realized after a few months of being in sales that I was often repeating the same thing over again, using the same thing to sell over and over again. And it's like, gosh, this isn't ideal for the customer because [inaudible 00:08:04] call me and ask these questions and get these answers and all this stuff. And it's not ideal for the company because they're paying commission on this every time. That's not going to be efficient for our growth. And because we were small, I was able to catch our GM and I was just like, "Hey, I've noticed this pattern where I'm repeating things over and over again and they're asking the same thing. (00:08:29): I think we should put that online. I think we should make that available so they can just see it and then buy it," because we had an online checkout process. And I was expecting him to be like, "Oh, well, I know it's important but for this [inaudible 00:08:46] another, we need to do it this way, and obviously you've thought all about it." And he goes, "Wait a minute, tell me more about that. What do you mean?" And by the end of the conversation he was like, "Hey, why don't you go do that? Why don't you go build that experience? Why don't you put that stuff in a self-serve flow?" (00:09:06): And we called it e-commerce manager and it was like got a growth before this growth, this is like 2010. But the core that learning was, your executive team and executive teams at companies are often very sharp, but the nature of their day-to-day just does not link them with customers. (00:09:34): And that means that over time, especially as a company grows, they often lose access to some of the best insights and in the heartbeat of the people who they're providing value to in contrast to folks that are closer to the problem. And so that means that your superpower is in really pulling those insights in and bringing them to life, staying close to the customer. There's not a single leader or executive that isn't going to be stoked to hear about valuable customer insights that highlight problems they might not be seeing. And there's a lot of those. So especially when they align to North Star metrics, those ones are the powerful ones. That was the way that I grew my career at Phil and I'm happy to share that journey too.

职业发展绝非一帆风顺，但确实存在一些行之有效的框架和方法。首先，我想先谈谈我最常看到人们用来推动职业发展的方法——但这种方法往往存在一些问题。比如，大多数人会拼命在现有职位和公司中努力提升自己，向上级展示自己的价值。我见过人们整理Excel表格，期待能在绩效评估中获益，或是努力提升自我主张能力，让同事或上司注意到自己的价值。这些努力固然值得肯定，但问题在于，你的晋升空间受限于上司的提拔能力，以及公司职位晋升的固有路径。更重要的是，外部环境可能与你的职业期望存在偏差——比如上司离职后，你不得不重新适应新领导。

我采用的方法是试图夺回主动权。我职业生涯初期在Bandwidth公司（现已上市）就偶然学到一个关键技巧。当时公司仅有50名员工，我加入时在销售部门工作，满怀激情却发现自己在重复同样的销售流程。这让我意识到，既不利于客户体验，也不符合公司利益。于是我找到GM，提议将重复内容上线自助服务——这项创新最终推动了公司增长。
不要将他们与客户割裂开来。（00:09:34）：这意味着随着时间推移，尤其是当公司规模扩大后，他们往往会失去获取最佳洞察的机会，无法深入了解那些他们正在为之创造价值的客户，而这些洞察本应来自最贴近问题根源的人群。因此，你的核心能力在于深入挖掘这些洞察并将其落地——始终紧贴客户需求。没有哪位领导或高管不会为听到能揭示他们未曾察觉问题的宝贵客户洞察而倍感振奋，这样的洞察数不胜数。特别是当这些洞察与北极星指标相契合时，其价值更是显而易见。这正是我在菲尔公司职业生涯成长的秘诀，我很乐意与大家分享这段历程。

turns.zh: 或许用一个简单的说法来回应你的观点，那就是开拓自己的道路。别总指望经理能为你规划最合理的路径，或是提供最大的机会。就提议说：“嘿，我觉得这可能是个更好的机会，我很想去尝试。” 如果你能举个Twilio的例子，那就更好了。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yeah. So when I joined Twilio, there was no growth team at all, not even a breath of it. I joined in product marketing and I was leading our product marketing for our messaging lines, but I followed the same guy that I just mentioned. I made it my own personal policy to like, hey, I'm going to do my job. And I'm going to do well, I'm going to keep notes of things I'm doing well and all that stuff because it's good, but I'm also going to get to know our customers. And I'm going to get to know our customers really well and I'm going to pay attention when I'm connecting with them, not just about the space I'm in, but just broadly what are some of the pain points and things they're articulating that are relevant to the business and what we're trying to get done. (00:13:00): And one of the things that came up was that users were struggling and folks were struggling to get started and use Twilio. And that contrasted so deeply to some of the things that our executive team was saying and had high conviction in our company had high conviction, which is that Twilio was so easy to use. In fact, it was top three things about Twilio that we were really trying to get out of their brand. Were so easy. Developers love us, they say we're so easy. And there were tweets coming all the time, developers saying like, "Oh my gosh, they got started in a couple of minutes." So there's all these things that made that compound and made that conviction stick. But as I was talking to customers, I was hearing a very different story and it made sense as we were penetrating new markets, adding more products, we were adding complexity and we were pulling in folks who were a little bit less motivated and those things contributed to people saying this is difficult. (00:13:55): And so at the time, this wasn't a 50 person in where I could just go to the floor and go to someone and be like, "Hey, there's this thing I heard about, I think we should do something." But there was another tactic that I could take, and I just started sharing a voice of the customer report. I started sharing my insights, started writing down and just sharing them. And it became with digest and eventually people were like, "Hey, can you share it with me? Can you share with me? Can you get on your list? Can share with me?" And this was in a few months of me joining, I was doing this. And then that turned into, "Hey, you should host a quarterly voice to the customer session or for all of product." And this was a request that was coming from some of the senior leaders at the company. (00:14:33): And when our Jeff Lawson is our CEO at the time heard about, he started attending too. So now in the session I started pulling in other people's insights too, because now they had a forum for this. I could do that and have people send that to me and I could compile it and all of these things. So then this established me as that person who knows about the customer even after short tenure. And then when came time to do annual planning that year, and I joined in 2014 at the end, so this is 2015, I pitched this idea, "Hey, we think that it's easy. It is not. Here's data that I have, the information that I have and I think that we need to start a growth team here and that needs to be a core focus." And I was able to bring in a really critical partner to that and other folks who could support that because I had built up some of that trust. (00:15:28): So by the time I was making that pitch, I had someone on Andre Crow who was the seventh hire at Twilio and got to number three on that spreadsheet or whatever who was really close to the CEO being like, "Yeah, we desperately need this." I'm seeing this. He led a website, he basically created the Twilio brand and he led all the website stuff and he is like, "Yeah, we definitely need this." So not only did I have that little bit of trust from the executive team, but I also had folks who were just trusted on their own advocating and supporting this that I was doing. And so it was approved just almost very easily. I put stuff together for it, but it was the meeting before the meeting had already been done by this other thing. So it helped me create the growth engineering, growth product team at Twilio.

是的。我加入Twilio时，公司根本没有增长团队，甚至连这个概念都闻所未闻。我最初负责产品营销，主管我们的消息产品线，但我一直追随我之前提到的那个领导者。我给自己定下一个原则：做好本职工作，记录自己做得好的地方。这固然重要，但更重要的是深入了解客户需求。我会仔细观察他们的痛点和诉求，确保这些信息能与我们的业务目标相契合。（00:13:00）  

很快我发现，用户在使用Twilio时遇到了诸多困难。这与我们高管团队的宣传口径形成了鲜明对比——他们坚称Twilio易于上手，甚至将“简单易用”列为品牌核心卖点。在社交媒体上，开发者们不断赞叹“几分钟就能上手”之类。但这些宣传与实际情况相差甚远。随着公司开拓新市场、推出新产品，复杂性增加，团队成员积极性下降，这些问题反过来加剧了用户的负面反馈。（00:13:55）  

当时公司规模还不到50人，没法直接召集大家开会讨论。但我采取了另一种策略——开始分享客户反馈报告，记录自己的见解并与同事分享。几个月后，这些报告引发了热议，人们纷纷询问：“能不能分享给我？”最终，产品团队要求每季度召开客户反馈会。时任CEO的杰夫·劳森也开始参与其中。（00:14:33）  

通过这些会议，我逐渐积累了客户洞察，并将其整合成正式报告。最终我成为公司内部公认的客户专家。2014年末加入后，2015年我便提议成立增长团队，将客户洞察作为核心工作重点。凭借与关键团队成员建立的信任，我成功争取到了支持。（00:15:28）
当时我离首席执行官说出“是啊，我们急需这个功能”已经很近了。我注意到他负责过一个网站，基本上开创了Twilio品牌，负责所有网站相关事务。他也表示：“没错，我们确实需要这个功能。” 所以我不仅获得了高管团队的一点信任，还有那些本身就备受信赖的人在为我所做的事情发声支持。因此，这个提案几乎轻而易举就获得了批准。我为此整理了相关材料，但那次会议之前，另一项工作已经完成了。这为我在Twilio建立增长工程和增长产品团队提供了助力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just how proactive your advice is here. There's a lot of people that don't do well and then just like, "Oh, I never had the opportunity or I kept got looked over all this time." And I love that there's all this just like, here's things you can be doing to get in front of people to provide value, to just create opportunity for yourself. Any other advice along the lines of just like, here's the things you could do for yourself versus waiting for someone to come and give you opportunity?
turns.zh: 我特别欣赏你在这里给出的积极主动的建议。很多人在工作中表现不佳时，总会找借口，比如“我从未得到机会”、“这些年来一直被忽视”。而你却能给出切实可行的方法，教人们如何主动展现价值、为自己创造机会。这类建议实在太棒了，远比坐等别人提供机会要有效得多。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's the most easily actual because to do all of our jobs, we need to know customers, we need to know about customer insights, product, we need to know. But then also customer facing teams, social, those want to crack into product. Your insights are extremely valuable. You're talking to customers every day more about their problems and their pain than a lot of other people do. And so that is by far and away to me the most powerful and accessible by anyone in any role in any space. But I'll also say that that broader concept of just, hey, there's things that, and things of value that you know that others can benefit from at your company and building your brand as someone that is supportive, smart, creative, able to solve problems, make sure that you're sharing that. And so maybe you're really freaking good at communicating with brevity. (00:17:35): I suck at that by the way. So more powered anyone that can do that, I'm actively working on it. So share that. Go to your general Slack channel or whatever and just be like, "Hey, just wrote some tips for how to do it, some ways that I am good at this." And those kinds of things can really go a long way towards people starting to view you as an SME and not just the space that you're in, but in broader areas. And that can always present open doors for you and other people are looking up to you and seeing you, someone who's strong in ways outside of just the role that you're in.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这才是最容易落地的。要做好我们的工作，必须了解客户，掌握客户洞察，熟悉产品。但同样，面向客户的团队，比如社交部门，也想深入了解产品。你的洞察力极其宝贵。你每天与客户打交道，了解他们的痛点和需求，这比大多数人做得都好得多。在我看来，这无论对任何职位、任何领域的人来说，都是最有价值、最容易获取的能力。不过我还要说更广泛的概念：你知道公司里有些有价值的信息，别人能从中受益。比如，你在品牌建设方面很有眼光，能帮助他人解决问题，那就一定要分享这些见解。也许你特别擅长简洁明了地沟通。（00:17:35）：说实话，我在这方面很糟糕。所以任何能做到这点的人都值得称赞，我正在努力改进。多分享这些心得。去公司的Slack群组或者其他平台，主动分享：“嘿，我总结了一些做事技巧，分享一下我的心得。”这样的举动会让人们逐渐把你视为某个领域的专家，而不仅仅局限于你所在的部门。这样做总能为你打开新机遇，别人会敬重你，视你为某个领域的行家，而不仅仅是某个职位的能手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: SME is a Subject Matter Expert, is that right?
turns.zh: SME是主题专家，对吧？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yes. Thank you for unpacking my acronyms. That's another thing that I am actively working on.
turns.zh: 是的。谢谢你解释我的缩写。这也是我在努力改进的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got you. I'll be on the lookout.
turns.zh: 明白了。我会注意的。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yes.

turns.en: Maybe one last question along these lines is do you have any advice for framing the proposal, framing an opportunity to your manager, higher ups that you see has worked best broadly?
turns.zh: 最后再问一个相关问题：对于向经理或上级提案或阐述机会，你有什么建议吗？你觉得哪些方法最有效？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And one thing I want to say too is with this stuff, I don't think that it necessarily does counter to what your manager's doing. It's more supporting them. I've done this stuff and then it's helped my manager promote me. So it's not necessarily, "Oh, we'll do this if your manager's failing you." Or they are not the boarding you or they can't support you. It's more like do this because this is going to be an accelerator for yourself irrespective of your manager. (00:18:55): But then also it'll be an accelerator for your manager in supporting you because one of the things that comes into play a lot when managers figure out promotions and doing those things is they'll sit in a room, often calibrations and with a bunch of people, and it makes it a lot easier when those people have had some access or exposure or whatever to you in a positive light. So these things can all run with your manager and not against, but it's just another way of you taking back the ability to build that momentum instead of relying on all of that going through one single other person.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。我还想说一点，关于这些事情，我觉得这并不一定与你的经理所做的工作相冲突。相反，这是在支持他们。我自己就做过这些事，最后还帮助我的经理提拔了我。所以这不一定是说，“哦，如果你的经理没能帮到你，我们就自己行动。”或者他们没有为你提供支持之类的。而是说，做这些事是因为这无论如何都会成为你自己的加速器，与你的经理无关。（00:18:55）但同样，这也会成为你经理支持你的加速器，因为当经理们决定晋升或做这些事情时，他们经常会和一群人坐在一起进行评估，而如果这些人对你有过积极的接触或了解，那会让事情变得容易得多。所以这些事情可以和你的经理携手共进，而非对抗。但这只是你重新夺回推动势头的另一种方式，而不是把一切都寄托在一个人身上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what I like about your second example is you just did it. You just started doing that tenant report for the company. It wasn't like, "Hey, I have a proposal, here's what I think you should do. Should we do it?"
turns.zh: 我喜欢你举的第二个例子，你就直接行动了。你就开始为公司做那个租户报告了。不是那种，“嘿，我有个提案，我觉得我们应该这么做。我们要不要试试？”

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's just like, yeah, just do it.
turns.zh: 就是，嗯，直接去做。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yeah, ungate your knowledge I think is the buzzword that I'm hearing.
turns.zh: 是啊，“释放你的知识”，我觉得这是我最近听到的一个流行词。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm. Never heard that.
turns.zh: 嗯。没听过这个。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: I think that's an Elena, see how many times we can bring her up. But you can do that within your own company. Everybody is skilled at things that they aren't explicit to their role or their space. And I think that ungating that opens opportunities. And if you're not sure, then go to my favorite go-to, which is talk to customers, get insights. Those are incredibly valuable. So rarely do people share those when they find them. So be the person that does that.
turns.zh: 我觉得这就是埃琳娜的观点，你看我们能提到她多少次了。但你可以在自己的公司里这么做。每个人都有擅长的事情，只是这些事情可能不属于他们的职责或工作领域。我觉得释放这些潜力能创造机会。如果你不确定，那就去找我最常推荐的办法——和客户交流，获取洞察。这些洞察非常宝贵。人们发现这些洞察后很少分享。所以就做那个敢于分享的人吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another area I want to chat about is experimentation and growth and data, which makes sense if strong perspectives is on being the new head of growth amplitude. So maybe we start with experimentation. You mentioned that there's a really interesting surprising result in an experiment you ran at Twilio that maybe changed your perspective on experimentation and what you think might work and not work.
turns.zh: 我想聊的另一个领域是实验、成长和数据，这很有意义，如果你的新头衔是增长副总裁的话。那么或许我们从实验开始。你提到在Twilio做的一个实验有非常有趣的惊人结果，也许这改变了你对实验的看法，以及你认为哪些方法可能有效，哪些可能无效。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: A hundred percent. Yeah, I'm through a fortune of two mind-blowing experiments that really shifted the way that I think about growth. So one of them, one of my favorite ones happened very early on at Twilio. So after I created this growth team, one of the things that I saw as to me an issue was that under signup flow, we just asked people for a username and an e-mail, like a password, and that was it. And that's actually relatively common at the time. This is a while ago now, everybody is [inaudible 00:21:16]. But we didn't, and actually there was a lot of existing conviction around that. I was like, "Hey, we retarding developers. Developers, they just want to do, they just want to get their hands on things. Don't put anything in their way, it's going to be disastrous. We don't want any shenanigans here with these folks, let's just let them in the gates." (00:21:33): But to me this was a really big assumption to make and a very costly one. It's like, okay, if that's the case, we're not going to know anything about anyone. And we didn't know who was signing up, we didn't know what they wanted to do. And that hurt our ability to understand how people were performing from a quantitative perspective. We were a little bit lost with prioritization. There's a number of implications here, but it's obviously a very contentious space. So this is the very first thing that I did and the first experiment that I ran. I did some research to understand say, okay, what are the most important questions to answer? What would I do really, really need to know? And it was stuff like what language are you coding in, what's your use case? What product you want to use? (00:22:14): And then there's one around, are you developer at all or were you use something else? Because there is rumors that we're having, not just developers sign up, which is this whole other interesting story. And I think of these questions that would also potentially be things that our developers signing up would understand why we're asking that it would feel natural. But anyway, again, adding anything to the signup was very contentious, but I really just wanted to get a little bit of data on it. So I wanted to run a test. I didn't have a team, I didn't have an engineering team yet and none of that stuff had built out. It was just me, myself and I. But like I said, I had started to build a little bit of trust and [inaudible 00:22:50], Andre, who I mentioned earlier who, because he was early employee and he had access to everything, one of those people, and he also was supportive of this and had similar haunches. (00:23:03): And so like the dead of the night, and by that, I mean 7:00 PM or something, I'm pretty sure it was a Friday. We just asked for forgiveness and put these questions into the signup flow and ran as Navy test with a small group. And I'm fully expecting, "Okay, this is going to hurt our numbers, but maybe it won't be so bad and I'm going to be prepared to advocate the power of this data that we're getting." I was totally thinking with written... Started to write the framework for how I wanted to surface this. And we start to get the data for this thing. I'm not kidding, an improved conversion. There's no personalization, nothing past it, just the questions. It improved conversion by 5%, just improved signups. And it was one of those like, "What? Okay, what is going on here?" And I actually dug into it, and what I found from just talking to a few customers once through the flow, I'm just learning about [inaudible 00:24:00] about it. (00:24:01): It was actually for folks, it was comforting. When you think about it, when users are signing up for your product for the very first time, it's new. This is new, that means it's scary. They're expecting it to be difficult. They're anticipating that there's going to be friction and challenges and that they're not going to figure it out. Almost like looking for the bogeyman. And that's the headspace. It's often the headspace that any of us are in when we're doing something new for the first time like ooh, this could be very challenging. And so by putting in these questions it's like, what's your language? It's like, "Oh, I do. I code a JavaScript and I can select that." Well, that's something I'm uncomfortable with. That would make my journey easier. Like "Yeah, bingo. That's my use case. Okay, I'm in the right place here." (00:24:51): It was actually giving folks something comforting and challenging the notion that this was going to be difficult, just the questions because it was aligning to some of the things that they were organically thinking about, which is what if they don't support my language? Or can I even do this use case I want to do? And so it was just a really interesting, the takeaway for me for this, the really interest takeaway was the psyche of the user is so, so critical. That's just as important as understanding your product and the broader market you're applying to and all those things. Just the psyche of users, new people doing things for the first time in your user flow, understanding that is powerful. And the simple catchy thing I say is that ultimately the learning here is, bad friction is bad, and good friction is good. There's no such thing as it being simple. It's just all friction is bad, which is what I had assumed going into this.
turns.zh:
百分之百。是的，我经历了两项令人惊叹的实验，它们真正改变了我对增长的看法。其中之一，也是我最喜欢的实验之一，发生在Twilio的早期阶段。在我组建增长团队后，我发现注册流程中存在一个问题——我们只要求用户输入用户名和邮箱，以及密码，仅此而已。这在当时确实很常见（毕竟是好久前的事了，现在大家都明白了）。但我们当时坚信这样做没问题。我当时想：“嘿，我们这是在阻碍开发者！开发者只想动手操作，不想有任何阻碍，否则后果不堪设想。我们不能在这群人身上搞这些花招，直接让他们进入就行了。” （00:21:33）但对我来说，这是一个极具风险的假设。试想一下，如果我们坚持这种做法，就无法了解用户的任何信息。我们既不知道谁在注册，也不知道他们的需求。这严重影响了我们从量化角度理解用户表现的能力。我们在优先级排序上也有些迷茫。这里涉及诸多影响因素，但显然这个问题争议很大。所以这是我做的第一件事，也是我开展的第一个实验。我做了些研究，思考哪些问题最重要？哪些信息我们真正需要？比如用户使用的编程语言、用例、希望使用的产品等。 （00:22:14）还有一个问题：你是开发者吗？还是在用其他产品？因为有传言说不只是开发者在注册，这背后还有个有趣的故事。我觉得这些问题对开发者来说是合理的，让他们觉得自然而然。但无论如何，在注册流程中添加任何额外信息都极具争议性，但我还是想收集些数据。于是我决定做个测试。当时我还没有团队，工程团队也尚未组建，一切都由我一人负责。但正如我所说，我已经开始赢得信任，[00:22:50]提到的安德烈就是其中之一。他是早期员工，可以访问所有数据，也支持我的想法，观点相似。 （00:23:03）于是我们挑了个深夜时段——我记得是周五晚上7点左右——悄悄地把这些问题加到注册流程中，用小规模测试进行验证。我满心期待：“好吧，这可能会影响转化率，但或许影响不大，我已经准备好为这些数据的价值据理力争了。” 我甚至开始构思如何呈现这些数据。结果数据出来了——转化率提升了5%！简直令人震惊。没有个性化设置，仅靠这些问题，转化率就提升了。我当时真是惊呼：“什么？！这到底怎么回事？” 我深入研究了一下，通过与少数用户交流，逐渐理解了其中的奥秘。 （00:24:01）这对用户来说，
这很令人安心。仔细想想，当用户首次注册你的产品时，对他们来说这是一件新事物。新鲜事物往往令人感到陌生和恐惧，他们会预期操作困难，预感会遇到阻碍和挑战，担心自己无法搞明白。这就像在寻找"可怕的怪物"——这就是用户的心理状态。这种心理状态在我们第一次尝试新事物时也很常见，比如"天啊，这可能很难"。因此，通过设计这些引导性问题，比如"你使用哪种语言？"，用户会回答"哦，我用JavaScript，可以选择这个选项"。这时用户会松一口气："原来如此，这正是我需要的。看来我来对地方了。"（00:24:51）这些问题实际上给了用户一种安心感，同时也挑战了他们认为操作困难的固有观念。用户会想："如果不支持我的语言怎么办？"或者"我能否实现我想实现的用例？"这些问题与用户自然产生的担忧相契合。比如，用户可能在想："如果不支持我的语言怎么办？"或者"我能否实现我想实现的用例？"因此，这些问题非常有趣。对我来说，最重要的启发在于用户的心理状态至关重要。这和理解产品、目标市场等同等重要。理解新用户在使用流程中的心理状态至关重要。我常说的一句话是，糟糕的阻碍是坏的，好的阻碍是好的。没有所谓的"简单"一说。只有所有阻碍都是坏的，而这正是我最初的误解。

turns.en: That the right way to do [inaudible 00:26:15] advocating for the engineers here is the right way to make any changes in production is through or with the approval of engineering, but it was the right move overall and definitely helped business, so yeah.

turns.en: Yeah, I love it. No, that's great. I like that move. I think we need more of that probably. I want to dig into what you actually... So what is it you changed, you added how many questions and then what were the questions?
turns.zh: 是的，我喜欢这个做法。太棒了。我觉得我们需要更多这样的尝试。我想深入了解你实际做了哪些改动，加了多少问题，然后这些问题具体是什么内容？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: There was a question around what language are you coding in? And then as an option to that, it was like, "Oh, I'm actually not coding, I'm not a developer." So for us, it actually gave us two really, really interesting data points. One was how many developers versus people who are not coding or in our flow? And then what language of the coding, which was massively helpful not just for growth and onboarding, but our documentation team, dos team. Would that end up being a critical way for us to gauge trends over time and catch things before whatever reports would come out at the end of the year, what people are doing, you start to see it. And then also product. What product are you interested in using? That was very critical for knowing the basics of how to organize someone's onboarding. Are you doing SMS? You're doing voice? To 281 or whatever. And then use case in use cases, you're doing a appointment reminders or are you doing a autoresponder or are you doing anonymous communications for a dating app or something. Right? So those were the very first questions.
turns.zh: 其中有一个问题是"你用哪种语言编程？"，然后作为选项，还有一个选项是"哦，我其实不编程，我不是开发者。"所以这实际上为我们提供了两个非常有趣的数据点。一个是开发者与不编程或不在我们流程中的人的比例。另一个是编程语言的选择，这对增长和入职流程非常有帮助，对我们的文档团队、开发运维团队也是如此。这最终会成为我们追踪趋势、在年底报告发布前发现问题的重要方式，你可以从中看出端倪。还有产品部分。你对哪个产品感兴趣？这对了解如何组织入职流程的基础知识非常重要。你用短信吗？你用语音吗？转接到281号码之类的。然后在用例方面，你是做预约提醒，还是自动回复，还是为约会应用做匿名通信之类的。对吧？这些就是最初的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, okay. So it was four dropdown questions and that increased conversion. I love these examples where friction and increased conversion... There's so few of them. You hear about this could work and it's rare. And so what did you take away? What's the pattern you took from this? There's the idea, it's good friction, but is there something that you're like, what is a sign of this is going to be good friction?
turns.zh: 哇，好。所以是四个下拉菜单问题，然后转化率提高了。我喜欢这些摩擦与转化率提升的案例……这样的例子太少了。你听说这个可能有效，但很少见。那么你从中学到了什么？你总结出了什么规律？有这个理念，适当的摩擦是好的，但有没有什么迹象能表明这会是有效的摩擦呢？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: There's still alleviated a problem. They alleviated the problem they had where they're coming in and worried that it was going to be difficult or that they weren't going to be able to figure it out, they weren't going to be able to get their footing. And I'd say that that's not unique to Twilio. That's something that I think users experience at any front door, at any company, any signup beginning the signup loads, it's like, "Here we go, buckle up." Especially when it's in a work context and there might be extra pressure on you to succeed or for you to make as an accurate assessment. So I think that psyche of, "Okay, am I in the right place? Is it's going to do what I need it to do? Can I figure it out? Am I capable?" These are extremely common things for people to feel when they're signing up. (00:28:48): And so certainly, that I think can carry out to any place. I'd encourage absolutely everybody to be putting those experiences within their early onboarding, not just for you selfishly, so you can learn and segment them appropriately, but also so the user can feel more confident as they get going and like, "Hey, I'm in the right place. This is going to do what I needed to do." But I think that the carry over there is just the psyche of the user and just being so aware that it's not so cookie cutter as, "What is the problem my market experience is and what can my product do to help them?" There's also this other thing in the room which is so important to people's success, their ability to succeed with your products and your self-serve experiences, which is, what is the mentality and the psyche of the person at the various stages in your journey? (00:29:37): And if you're not incorporating that or addressing that, you will absolutely miss things or things will fail and you'll be very confused as to why. We had a great experiment that I'm happy to talk about where same concept, a totally different situation, which is later in onboarding. One of the things that we tried to do over time to make Twilio less complex was to offer steps like, [inaudible 00:30:08] onboarding, welcome step one, here's what you want to build. Great, we all know that now, "Okay, step one, go do this thing. Step two, go to this thing. Three, this thing. Four, this thing. Five, bam, you're live, congratulations, aha," all these things. So we shipped that, got that out there and I was like, yeah, it was improved conversion. It wasn't like that great. It's like, man. We went from there being absolutely nothing, "Choose you're adventure, figure it out, go figure it out. Good luck." To this prescriptive thing. And it wasn't converting [inaudible 00:30:37]. (00:30:38): So to talk to some users and there wasn't anything particularly obvious that was coming out as to what the issue was. It was like, "Oh yeah, Let's go to step one." And we did mock the people. "Okay, now I know, I do step two." But there was one thing that I was hearing that was coming out that feels like something, and that was the telephone number, the telecom part. Developers when they were coming into Twilio, it was things that were familiar to them. APIs, the language they're coding in, code samples, documentation, things like the bogeyman, the things that would psychologically trip them up, telecom, phone numbers. These things that just were completely out of the zone of anything that they'd ever worked with before, especially earlier on in Twilio's journey. (00:31:28): But even now, right? Telecom's very different beast for most developers. And guess what was step one? Get a phone number because that's step one. Anytime that anyone's trying to teach one to use Twilio one-on-one, always going to sit down, ask and be like, "Okay, here we're going to go get a phone number and configure it." And that's what anyone every time will do. However, in a self-serve experience, when you don't have that safe person sitting next to you being like, "Don't worry, it's going to be okay, I'm going to take you through this crazy telecom journey." They're on their own, but that's psyche telling is them like, "Oh my god, telecom. Well, I can't do that. That sounds scary. We're getting a phone number configured. Whoa, I'm out of my debt." (00:32:01): And so what did we do to test this out? Test out whether that was the issue? Actually, and it's first we're in the MVP. They kicked them out of the portal entirely and put them into a docs page where we could manufacture an experience where the first thing they saw was code and they're in the docs safe place, the language that they're coding in and then snuck in there. (00:32:26): It was like, "Oh, get a phone number, let's go configure it." Not as step one, not as the leading thing, but embedded. And the analogy I have for this is pilling a hot dog. So if anyone's got a dog or an animal you have to feed a pill to, it's like you can't just feed the pill to the animal, it's never going to happen. But if you shove it inside of a hot dog, which looks good and that's exciting, then you can get them to consume it more easily. And so this was-
turns.zh:
问题仍然存在。他们解决了之前遇到的难题——用户注册时会感到困惑，担心操作复杂或无法上手，难以适应新环境。我认为这并非Twilio独有的问题，任何公司、任何产品入门流程都会面临类似挑战，特别是当用户处于工作场景中，面临更高成功压力或准确评估需求时，他们会产生诸多心理波动，比如"我是否选对了平台？产品能否满足需求？我能否顺利上手？"这些都是用户注册时极易产生的情绪反应。

（00:28:48）：这种心理效应在任何场景都适用。我建议大家在早期入门流程中融入这些体验，不只是为了自身学习和精细化分析，更要让用户充满信心："我找对了地方，产品能满足需求。"但更关键的是，用户的心理状态并非千篇一律，不能简单归结为"市场痛点是什么，产品如何解决"。还有一个至关重要的因素——用户在不同阶段的心理转变。（00:29:37）：如果忽视这些心理因素，项目必将失败且难以理解原因。我们曾进行过一个成功实验（涉及后期入门流程），通过分步骤引导解决了同类问题。比如，提供分步骤指南："欢迎加入，第一步……"但转化效果并不理想。我们发现用户仍在茫然中摸索，尽管流程看似清晰，但实际转化率低得令人失望。

（00:30:38）：通过用户访谈，我们发现问题并非显而易见。用户会说："好的，我知道第一步了。"但模拟演示后，他们还是会卡在电信部分——电话号码、运营商接口等对开发者而言完全陌生的领域。这正是Twilio早期阶段用户面临的心理障碍。
这是第一步。每次有人想一对一教别人使用Twilio时，他们总会先坐下来，问道："好的，我们现在要去获取一个电话号码并进行配置。"而这也是所有人每次都会做的。然而，在自助服务体验中，当你身边没有可靠的人指导你时——"别担心，一切都会顺利的，我会带你完成这个复杂的电信配置流程。"——用户只能独自面对。这种心理暗示会让他们想："天哪，电信配置？我可做不到，这太吓人了。我们要配置电话号码？啊，我还是算了。"（00:32:01）那么我们是如何验证这个问题的呢？我们首先在最简可行产品（MVP）阶段，把用户完全踢出门户，引导他们进入文档页面。在这里，用户首先看到的是代码示例，处于安全的文档环境中，使用他们熟悉的编程语言，之后再自然地引入相关功能。（00:32:26）就像是把药丸藏进热狗里。如果你要给狗或其他动物喂药，直接喂药丸根本行不通。但如果你把药丸塞进热狗里，看起来美味又吸引人，用户就更容易接受了。这就是我们所做的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. We do peanut butter, that's [inaudible 00:32:55].
turns.zh: 是的。我们做的是花生酱，[00:32:55，声音不清晰]。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yeah, exactly, right? Yeah, hot hotdog, peanut butter, all that. You bury it. You embed the scary unpleasant thing. And so that's what you said with the phone number stuff, that telecom stuff. And guess what? Even though we're a good amount of the console and they're going off and we had no easy return button, it converted better because we were addressing the big problem that was there at the time, which is their psyche. They were not ready to come in and immediately thrown into a phone number experience. That was letting the bogeyman and out to party and that's not what was going to work. We needed to put that bogeyman pill and the hotdog. (00:33:31): And so then once that validated, then we can actually go through the business of putting that into the onboarding float correctly and then that could be even better. But so again, the psyche of your user is such a critical thing to be thinking about. And if something very logical isn't converting well sometimes, it means that you're battling against the psyche of a user and you want to take a step back and think about and learn about where someone is psychologically in your space.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错，对吧？比如热狗、花生酱之类的。你把那些不受欢迎的东西埋起来。那就是你说的电话号码那块，电信相关的部分。猜猜怎么着？尽管我们在控制台上下了不少功夫，他们情绪激动，我们又没有简单的返回按钮，但转化效果还是不错的，因为我们解决了当时用户面临的核心问题——他们的心理负担。他们还没准备好一进来就面对电话号码的体验。这就像放出“洪水猛兽”，但这样做根本行不通。我们需要先安抚用户的恐惧情绪，再推出热狗策略。（00:33:31）一旦验证成功，我们就能正确地将其整合到新用户引导流程中，效果会更理想。但关键是，用户的心理状态是必须重点关注的。有时候再合理的方案如果转化不佳，说明你正在与用户的心理抗衡。这时候你需要退一步，深入理解用户在你产品中的心理状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Feels like you had this experiment that was a complete redesign of the onboarding flow and that didn't work. And then your second attempt was a different approach that's like a full onboarding flow. And I'm curious, do you have a take on just when you run experiments? And it's something we dealt with a lot at Airbnb in other places is like, do you just redesign the whole thing or is it better to iteratively work from where you're today and just experiment piece by piece towards some future much better experience?
turns.zh: 感觉你们做了个实验，完全重构了引导流程，结果却不理想。然后第二次尝试用了不同的方法，整个引导流程重新设计。我很好奇，你们在做实验时是怎么考虑的？在Airbnb和其他公司，我们也经常遇到这种情况：是彻底重构整个流程，还是从现有基础上逐步迭代，再逐步优化？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Here's what I would say to this is that from a high level, it's always going to be better to be iterative. And the reason that it's better is that roughly 80% of the times, ORs in the time are hypotheses and the things that we believe will be true [inaudible 00:34:42]. And this is amazing. There's an amazing article out there I'm happy to share with you so you can put in the show notes.
turns.zh: 我的看法是，从高层角度看，迭代总是更优的。原因在于，大约80%的情况下，假设都是错误的，而这些假设是基于我们主观认知的。（00:34:42，声音不清晰）这真的很神奇。我这里有篇很棒的文章，愿意分享给你们，可以放在节目笔记里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: That really takes a scientific approach to proving that out. Companies like Netflix and Microsoft, there's over and over again 80 plus percent. Some companies say 90% of things fail. And so the closer you get to something that you go bear your head in the sand or go into an attic and build something for six months and ship it, the more likely it is that you are going to ship the 80% wrong stuff. (00:35:17): Whereas the more iterative you are, the more likely that you're going to catch it sooner. And failure doesn't have to be a wall, it can be a compass, it can be the thing that leads you to the right thing. And so you always want to as best you can, get stuff in front of customers so that you can get that compass and get that compass activated, know where to go. (00:35:40): So that means doing ugly things. I tell my teams all the time, if it's not embarrassing, you've gone too far. Got to be embarrassing. The first thing, that was embarrassing, kicking people out, onboarding, spend all this money and whatever to get them into your center flow, and then the first thing we do, get out of here. That's nuts. But if it hadn't validated, that would've been a very cheap but very valuable learning. Instead, it was a very powerful cheap learning in the other direction. Okay, now we know we can invest in it. We know that's the right thing to do. So always better to be iterative so that you are letting failure work for you instead of having it be a trap that you fall into.
turns.zh: 确实需要用科学的方法来验证这一点。像Netflix和微软这样的公司，成功率往往超过80%。有些公司声称90%的项目都会失败。因此，当你急于完成某个项目时，比如埋头苦干六个月后仓促上线，很可能最终推出80%有缺陷的产品。而如果能更频繁地迭代，往往就能更早发现问题。失败不应是障碍，而应成为指引的方向标，帮助你找到正确的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that you just shared as per experiment, you're probably wrong 80% of the time. In my experience, launching a halt redesign is as negative a hundred percent of the time. I've grown weary to avoid that as much as possible, which is like, you know that, you're taught that as you go into growth and product, but you're just like, "Nah, come on, let's just make it awesome. Just redesign this whole thing." Especially your designers is always like, "No, let's start again. Let's make it amazing." turns.zh: 我知道你刚分享的实验结果显示，80%的情况下你很可能是错的。以我的经验来看，推出一项大改版产品，失败的概率几乎是百分之百。我现在越来越避免这样做，因为这太容易出错了。在产品和增长团队中，你肯定听过这样的忠告，但有时你还是会想：“不行，我们一定要把它做得超棒，彻底重新设计整个界面！” 尤其是设计师总会说：“不，我们从头再来，一起创造惊喜！”但结果往往不尽如人意，最后只能匆忙上线，因为再来一次已经来不及了。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Well, it's funny, in the articles, and you'll see it was written by somebody from Microsoft who built Implementation platform and did all these cool things, as he went into actually trying to apply a scientific method of figuring out how often people are wrong about their hypotheses and what they're planning to do. He's like, "I wonder if that applies to us here at Microsoft." Even for him, that question of [inaudible 00:37:16]. And I think it's challenging when there's a lot of smart people in this space doing things and it's very difficult to think, "Gosh, am I really wrong? 80 plus, 90% of the time?" But when you think about it, makes total sense because what has to happen for something to be successful? You have to understand the problem perfectly. You have to then understand who's having the problem perfectly, the customer. At what time they're having the problem. (00:37:43): Then you've got to put the right solution in front of them to solve that problem. Maybe you've got the problem, all that stuff, but your solution something off. Or maybe your solution is right, but maybe it's just not presented, it communicated in the right way. You could have any one of those things off and it's not going to succeed. It's not going to have the metric impact you're expecting it to have. So in that context, it's almost like incredible. We do succeed 20 to 10% of the time given everything that has to line up. And so I think it's one of those things where you really want to go into it embracing that, "Okay, this isn't about how smart I am or how good my team is or any of that stuff. It's just the logic of this is challenging to get it right and let's embrace that and let's lean into that knowledge and make it a part of our strategy," instead of finding against it.
turns.zh: 嗯，这挺有趣的。在那篇文章里，你会发现作者是微软的一位工程师，他开发了实施平台，完成了许多了不起的工作。当他开始尝试运用科学方法来研究人们对假设的误解频率以及后续的行动时，他不禁自问：“这套方法对我们微软也适用吗？”即便对他来说，这个问题也颇具挑战性。毕竟，这个领域里有很多聪明人都在努力探索，而要思考“天哪，我真的错了吗——80%甚至90%的情况下都是如此？”实在不易。但仔细想想，这完全说得通。毕竟，要想让某项创新成功，必须做到哪些关键点呢？首先，你得彻底理解问题所在；其次，要准确把握目标客户的痛点；还要精准把握他们遇到问题的场景。（00:37:43）然后，你必须为他们提供合适的解决方案。可能技术方案本身没问题，但呈现方式存在缺陷；又或许方案本身没错，但缺乏有效的沟通。只要其中任何一个环节出错，创新都注定失败，无法达到预期的效果。因此，在这种情况下，成功率达到20%至10%简直令人惊叹。考虑到所有环节都必须精准对接，这份成功实在难能可贵。所以我认为，我们应该坦然接受这个现实：“这与个人的智慧、团队的能力无关，关键在于理解这套逻辑的挑战性。让我们欣然接受这种挑战，深入钻研相关知识，将其融入我们的战略体系中”，而不是与之抗衡。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: So here's the thing, I think there's very little that we can do to make that space easier. All those things have to be figured out. And so I definitely think that everybody is going to be in a space where their original ideas, untested ideas are going to be around that hit rate. (00:39:47): So all of that is extremely expensive. If you've got a designer, create those mocks for that experience, put it in front of people, see how they engage with it. That can be so powerful. Let's fail fast by using those tools rather than figuring out a way that you can rise above where everyone else is operating and figure out ways to solve all that complex stuff better because that's going to be challenging, but you can always get better at experimenting and validating things faster.
turns.zh: 事情是这样的，我觉得我们能让这个过程更容易的办法微乎其微。所有这些问题都需要去逐一解决。所以我坚信，每个人都会面临这样一个阶段——他们最初的想法、未经验证的创意，都需要通过转化率来检验。然而，验证这些想法的方式可以大不相同，你可以快速验证这些创意，这才是关键所在。A/B测试是验证实验最昂贵的方式之一，通常需要设计、工程团队的投入，还要由产品经理、增长团队或市场人员来策划。这些投入都需要大量时间，即便只是简单的事情也不例外。再加上时间因素——我需要运行多久才能看到效果？（00:39:47）所以所有这些都成本极高。所以我认为关键在于深入思考：“好的，我能做些什么来快速验证我们的这些想法呢？”你可以借助“彩绘门”（painted doors）来实现，即在创意尚未成型前就测试概念和想法，而不是等实际产品出来后再测试。你可以制作模型。如果有设计师，就为体验创建这些模型，展示给用户，看看他们如何与之互动。这会非常有效。（00:40:16）在这一阶段，你可以否定大量假设。只有到了深度A/B测试阶段，或者在验证过程中不断优化的阶段，你才能降低失败率。因为你通过其他方法更快地失败，所以我更倾向于这种方法。让我们借助这些工具快速失败，而不是想方设法超越他人的操作水平，努力更好地解决所有复杂问题。虽然这很具挑战性，但你总能在实验和验证方面做得更快。

（00:43:47）：但对于我们这些负责用户转化和升级销售的团队来说，我们幸运地没有这样的压力。我们可以充分利用这一优势。因此，在某些情况下，我会主张、推动并亲自使用更低的置信区间。比如，如果这能让一年内能多做一倍的实验，那何乐而不为呢？归根结底，这些都是验证假设的方法。如果在某个角色中使用95%的置信率，你其实是在接受5%误判的风险。多做一些实验，多挑战自己，多积累经验。最终，当你回顾团队或个人一年来的成果时，你会发现其积极意义。

turns.en: So I'll say this, this is actually very critically important. You must have this game plan set before you run something. And always, always, always, if you're going to accept more risk of a false success or false positive, false negative, you want to then be really thinking about how you're going to harden your validation of a hypothesis. (00:46:03): For example, let's take that when we talked about with Twilio where we are kicking people out and we're sending them to the pilling hotdog experiment, and we're sending people to that experience to hide the phone number. Now in that case, let's say that we were going to accept a lower confidence interval. I would very much want to see qualitative feedback to confirm that that hypothesis was true. I want to be looking at the qualitative data from the ones where people were thrown into the existing flow and one's put into the dogs that one of them felt more confident and more like this was really easy to get through and they felt out of a territory and things like that. Like, "Figure this out, but it feels like it's that amount of my depth." (00:46:52): I would want to be looking for other things to corroborate the hard data that I'm seeing. And yes, it opens the door to whenever you open the door to more risk acceptance, you are going to have some false successes there. (00:47:51): If you just run 10 in a year on there, maybe two around impact, two of a course of an entire year if you take that approach. But I think some of the methods that I use can sound at the service level as more like, "Oh, I'm going by my gut." turns.zh: 接下来我要说的是，这一点其实非常关键。在开展任何项目之前，你必须先制定好游戏计划。很多团队会陷入的一个误区是，他们先开展实验或其他行动，然后再让数据去适应假设。或者有时候他们甚至没有明确的假设，只是说"这能让我们的指标更优化"，但却没有真正理解我们测试的核心原因。这正是我们容易陷入的另一个陷阱。"比如，'让我们[不可听清00:45:36]用80%的置信区间吧。反正我觉得这样挺好的。那个叫劳拉的人说这很棒。'"这种想法永远是个陷阱。因此，我们必须提前深思熟虑，明确"我们将如何验证这个假设"。（00:46:03）：以Twilio为例，我们让用户进入'隐藏电话号码'的实验。当时，如果我们接受较低的置信区间，我会非常希望看到定性反馈来确认假设是否成立。我会关注那些被扔进现有流程和进入实验组的用户的反馈。前者可能更自信，觉得流程更顺畅；后者则可能抱怨"我被困住了"之类的问题。（00:46:52）：我还会寻找其他数据来印证硬数据。比如，接受更高风险时，难免会有误判。但综合所有信息，能更大程度地确保我们推送给用户的功能对客户真正有益。再怎么强调都不为过：一年内不尽可能多地推出新功能，本身就是巨大的风险，尤其是在失败率如此之高的情况下。因此，我对数据科学家们（我曾与其中一些交流过）强调，80%的置信区间数据清晰地揭示了不进行充分实验的危害。（00:47:51）：如果一年只进行10次实验，其中两三次涉及影响力评估，那么全年产出将大打折扣。数据科学家会理解："如果我们这样做，增加实验次数，成功率就能翻倍或三倍，最终带来积极成果。"你仍然可以向数据科学家解释背后的逻辑。再次强调，这正是为什么作为数据驱动型从业者，当你被问及为何要这样做时，我会说："这只是凭直觉判断。"但数据驱动其实就是要直面那些我们未必深知或未曾意识到的硬数据现实——比如那惊人的失败率。

（00:50:55）：对此，我想说的是，增长团队向外部人员传授知识至关重要，尤其是让非增长部门和领导增长团队的人明白，增长团队成功的唯一途径就是接受他们存在的局限性——验证机遇、识别核心挑战并全力以赴。这绝非每周甚至每月就能完成的任务，这取决于所在行业的现状和未知因素。因此，任何受短期胜负和改进指标束缚的增长团队都注定会陷入危险境地。这类环境容易催生虚荣指标和数据粉饰的现象。更成功的团队往往会延长报告周期。因为只要给予增长团队足够的时间去失败、去学习正确的做事方法，他们就一定能取得真正的成功，不是那种“好吧，让数据符合预期”的表面成功，而是实实在在的指标提升。

（00:52:03）：所以，必须向外部人员普及这个理念。如果你发现自己被短期指标束缚，分享那个80%的失败率数据吧。这只是数学、统计学和数据的问题。在短期内你可能无法成功，但长期来看一定可以。这就是我最想强调的一点。在Twilio和后续的Rapid公司，我花了大量时间在增长团队上，我相信在Amplitude也会继续投入，帮助大家理解什么才是最健康、最强大的增长团队生态系统。而时间和预期的管理是其中的关键。

And then make sure that you're orienting your experience of product around those people.

人工智能驱动的SLG和PLG模式之间。是的，我认为它们本质上是一枚硬币的两面——产品增长和销售。对我来说，这两者在主题上非常相似。不同之处在于，增长模式下你通过产品本身进行销售，而销售模式则需要以一对一的方式直接与客户互动。因此，企业需要同时运用这两种力量，才能最优地转化目标用户。如今的市场环境下，用户既希望被产品说服，也希望获得企业级服务，而大型企业往往通过人性化服务来达成目标。企业需要深入理解用户需求，量身定制解决方案，否则就会错失良机。因此，我认为这两种力量必须协同运作，效果才会显著。（01:00:06）：关键在于，尝试突破PLG模式的公司面临的最大挑战，往往在于如何从根本上适应这一新领域。用户的需求、所处阶段以及心理诉求都至关重要。许多公司会这样想：“好吧，我们要尝试PLG模式。就把现有的企业级销售方案拆分一下，去掉一些功能，调整定价策略，争论十美元、九美元还是75美元，最后某个人拍板决定。”但这种讨论往往聚焦于产品层面（01:00:58）：我们该如何利用产品？如何打破壁垒，引入并转化这些用户？但我认为最容易被忽视的关键点是，当我们从销售模式向PLG模式转型时，必须进行彻底的重置。我们需要认识到，这本质上也是销售——通过产品实现销售。优秀的销售代表在与客户沟通时，会深入理解对方的问题所在。因此，我们也需要做到这一点：进入自助服务模式的用户存在哪些独特的痛点？以Amplitude这样的公司为例，许多尝试PLG策略的团队都希望达成多个目标，但核心诉求之一是开拓中小微市场，为初创企业提供落地与成长的平台。（01:01:57）：关键在于理解他们的挑战和独特需求，因为我们要用产品来解决这些问题。我们必须站在用户的角度，理解他们面临的具体问题。通过在多家初创公司任职及提供咨询服务的经验，我发现一个普遍现象：很少有初创公司能配备足够的分析师来满足需求。实际上，很多公司甚至根本没有分析师。这意味着CEO不得不亲自分析数据为董事会制作仪表板，产品经理则要独自解析产品数据。（01:02:34）：这种角色错位的现象普遍存在——人们被困在既定的职位中，既要承担分析师的职责，又要负责产品开发。
分析师们也是如此。我认为这尤其困扰着初创公司和早期阶段的企业。当他们审视自身心理时，他们在乎什么？当他们为产品分析或其他需求发送数据时，他们在思考什么？他们在寻找能让他们安心的方法——确保能准确解析关键指标，生成正确呈现数据的报告。如何最佳呈现用户流失率？肯定有最佳方法，毕竟很多人都在做这件事。猜猜怎么着？确实有一些非常有效的方法，也有成功为董事会搭建仪表板的案例。（01:03:16）许多现有框架（如基准测试）中都蕴含着这类知识。这些数据真的可靠吗？因此，我认为如果我们从这个角度出发，理解问题的根源，就能采取多种措施真正改变自助式体验的运作方式，帮助用户转化，并向他们展示Amplitude如何赋予他们强大的分析能力。但我认为所有公司（不只是Amplitude）在转型过程中都需要注意的一点是，切勿将其视为简单复制粘贴的工作，必须拆解核心要素。在制定策略时，切勿从产品出发，而应从客户、用户、潜在客户——即将进入你的产品生态的人群——入手。确保理解他们的痛点与销售端客户的需求有何不同，并围绕这些人群设计产品体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that you almost have to start again as a product company, as a product because you may need to solve completely different problems that eventually lead to the same place. But it's interesting what you're saying that you may end up targeting analysts or PMs. I know Amplitude or has always focused on PMs, but-
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，作为一家产品公司，你几乎得从头再来一次，因为你可能需要解决完全不同的问题，最终却殊途同归。但你提到可能会把目标客户锁定为分析师或产品经理，这点很值得探讨。我知道Amplitude一直专注于产品经理，但——

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Yeah, it's right. And there's always nice thing about it is it's in some ways, it does feel like you're starting fresh because you do need to start with the customer again and what's their problem. But in a lot of ways, you can carry over a lot of the same knowledge. At that point you know what's working well. Amplitude for example, does have a ton of knowledge around what some of the best ways artists set up reports. There's a lot of things that they have the momentum going, like where do you choose that momentum and how do you put that and curate that in front of users and make sure that they're getting the right things. There's a ton of momentum already there. It's just a little bit about harnessing it and understanding like, yeah, where are the gaps because there are going to be gaps. (01:05:08): But anchoring in a customer problem as I think the way that you start any new product, any new thing that you're releasing, should always think about the customer and the pain point. So no different than when you're doing PLG for the first time or cracking into it. You need to be thinking again, starting again with the problem, the problems they have, the psyche that they have coming to your space so that you can build something that is going to effectively make them feel like, "Oh you can solve my problem, you get me." And show them how your product's going to do that.
turns.zh: 是啊，这说得对。其中一个好处是，在某种程度上，确实感觉像是重新开始，因为你需要再次从客户需求出发，了解他们的问题所在。但在很多方面，你又能迁移许多已有的知识储备。在那个阶段，你已经清楚哪些方法行之有效。比如Amplitude就积累了大量关于艺术家如何设置报告的最佳实践经验。还有很多既有优势，比如如何抓住这些势头，并将其呈现给用户，确保他们能获得正确的信息。这些优势已经存在，关键在于如何加以利用，并理解其中的空白之处（因为空白总会存在）。（01:05:08）但归根结底，客户需求应该是任何新产品、新功能开发的起点。无论是首次尝试PLG模式，还是切入新领域，都需要从客户痛点出发，理解他们的需求和心理诉求，这样才能打造出让他们感叹“哦，你能解决我的问题，你懂我”的产品，并向他们展示产品如何做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, and this is around developers. You worked at Twilio, obviously Twilio sold developers. I think Rapid where you work right before Amplitude also sold developers. Selling to developers feels like such a hot space right now. There's so many startups that are just building developer tools, such a huge market. Used to be not. Used to be like there's not a market in developers. They're not going to spend money, there's not enough of them. And now it is a big popular spot. And so I'm curious, what have you learned about building a startup and a product that sells to developers? I imagine a lot of founders building search tools would be really curious.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题是关于开发者的。你曾在Twilio工作，显然Twilio面向开发者销售产品。Rapid（你加入Amplitude之前所在的公司）也做过类似业务。现在面向开发者的产品销售似乎很火爆，涌现出许多开发者工具初创公司，这个市场规模巨大。过去可不是这样，人们认为开发者市场没有需求，他们不愿花钱，也不认为开发者数量充足。但现在这已成为热门领域。我很好奇，你在开发面向开发者的初创产品和产品时，有哪些经验值得分享？我想很多开发搜索工具的创业者会对此很感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: The first is that developers are just a very different audience from any others. I've seen so many people who have come in strong on growth really well or product really well with other audiences and like, "Oh, I'm going to take all those learnings, I'll pivot into serving developers." And as it being a very steep climb because developers are so different. And let me give you a couple just fun facts that make them really different. And some of these have some interesting stories. One is developers, almost two, one, do not look at your marketing website at all. They go straight to your signup flow. So what that means is all that beautiful context that you're setting and the product aid pricing, all that stuff, very often they're skipping all of it context free and going straight to your signup. And so anytime you make an assumption like, "Oh, well, they probably know this coming in to signup." Or like, "Well, we don't need to include, that's on the marketing website." None of that's going to apply to this group of people. (01:07:15): They're there. The analogy I have for this group is they're the IKEA buyers who when IKEA package comes, they're not opening up the instruction manual and reading in and then starting to go through, they're in there tearing open the bags and starting to pull the pieces together and trying to build it. They'll come up for context and steps and such when they get stuck if they're motivated. So that's one thing. And then another one is just the aversion to talking to sales. And I think hearing that, some they're like, "Oh yeah, well, I hate sales too." When I'm sent out and get bombarded by sales, that's the worst. I totally get that. But developers are on this whole other level. There was a fang company sign up for Twilio, built a POC, launched to production, all this, and operated in that space for months without engaging once with sales. (01:08:12): I was trying to reach them and I ended up being the one that talked to them first because they reached out to support because there was something about their delivery that was off ,there missing a feature and they did not want to talk to sales. They ended up talking to me when I was in product marketing. And that was my first exposure of like, these people not want to talk to sales. And then there's another one where a giant retail company where the engineering team signed up with their personal e-mail addresses so they wouldn't get bombarded by sales. It was only later that we found out. Anyway. But the thing that's most important, these are fun facts, but the thing that I would say is the most important, the thing to leave with listeners here is what makes them so different? (01:08:54): Why? What's the deal here? And it stems from their charter and their responsibility. So if we put ourselves in developer's shoes for a minute, a developer, if a developer is required to use your product, especially if they're the primary user, the primary builder, it's really important to recognize that they're responsible for that. If your service goes down, that's their responsibility. Not just for themselves but their team. If the pager wakes up someone because the service they bought from you goes down, that's on them. If, oh, it turns out that doesn't work with the systems that they said it was, well, that's on them. Doesn't integrate with the data the way that everyone wanted it to? That's on them. Everyone lives to developer when it's not working right and it cannot work right. In so many ways, that's their failure, it can cost them their job, it could cost them the trust to their team. (01:09:50): It cost them their reputation. And that means that the stakes are very high for them every time that they're adopting something new. So they can't afford to take someone's word for it. Especially a sales rep who might have some other motivations from their perspective, they can't afford to trust your content or someone's word. They must do it. They must prove it themselves. And so that's why, for developers to be bought in, they need to do something, build something, a proof of concept at the very least, if not moving further than that. And so that means they're going to be pretty darn deep in their self-serve experience with you before they're ready to commit. And so if you are a company that is providing, that requires developers to build, you must invest in self-serve experiences in order to effectively convert your audience. And you should be thinking of them. Something akin your self-serve function and growth folks, someone akin to Salesforce because your developers are not going to accept sales coming in and trying to convert them at that stage.
turns.zh:
首先，开发者群体与其他受众截然不同。我见过许多人在面向其他受众时，无论是增长策略还是产品设计都做得非常出色，然后就想：“哦，我要把这些经验应用到服务开发者上。”但这实在是难上加难，因为开发者太过独特。让我举几个有趣的例子说明他们的不同之处，其中有些还有趣的故事。第一个例子是，开发者几乎从不看你的营销网站。他们直接跳到注册流程。这意味着你精心设置的所有背景信息、产品定价等内容，他们往往会跳过这些直接进入注册环节。所以当你假设“他们注册前应该了解这些信息”或者“这些内容都在营销网站上”时，对这群人根本不适用。

（01:07:15）：他们就是这样的。我给这个群体打个比方，他们就像宜家买家。当宜家包裹送达时，他们不会先翻阅说明书再动手，而是直接撕开包装袋，开始组装家具。遇到困难时，他们才会去查找步骤说明。所以，假设他们有问题需要帮助，除非主动去寻求，否则他们不会主动寻求帮助。

另一个例子是他们对销售人员的厌恶。我知道有些人会说：“哦，我也讨厌销售人员。”当我被派去面对狂轰滥炸的销售攻势时，那简直是最糟糕的经历。我完全理解他们的感受。但开发者的情况更极端。有个大型科技公司注册了Twilio服务，完成了POC测试，成功上线并运营数月，却从未与销售人员有过任何沟通。

（01:08:12）：我试图联系他们，最终却成了第一个与他们对话的人，因为他们向支持部门求助，称某个功能缺失却不愿与销售人员沟通。当时我在产品营销部门，第一次意识到开发者不愿与销售沟通的现象。还有个大型零售公司，工程团队用个人邮箱注册账户，只为避免被销售人员骚扰。直到后来我们才发现真相。

但最重要的是，这些趣事背后的本质原因在于他们的职责与使命。设身处地为开发者考虑，如果他们必须使用你的产品，尤其是作为主要用户和开发者，他们会深刻意识到自己对产品的责任。服务中断是他们的过错，不仅对自己，对团队也是如此。服务故障导致警报通知被触发，责任归他们。产品与预期系统不兼容，责任归他们。数据集成不达标，责任归他们。当产品无法正常运行时，所有人都会追究开发者的责任。开发者是最后的防线——如果产品无法正常运行，责任全在他们身上。这可能导致他们丢掉工作，甚至危及职业生涯。
他们信任自己的团队。（01:09:50）：这让他们失去了声誉。这意味着，每当他们采用新技术时，风险都极高。因此，他们不能轻易相信别人的承诺。尤其是销售代表，可能出于自身利益考量，他们更不愿轻易相信你的内容或他人的说辞。开发者必须亲自验证。正因如此，要想让开发者买账，他们必须拿出成果，至少要构建一个概念验证模型，甚至不止于此。这意味着，在开发者真正下定决心之前，他们必须深入体验你的自助服务流程。因此，如果你的公司要求开发者参与技术开发，就必须投资打造自助服务体验，才能有效转化目标用户。这一点值得你重点关注——你的自助服务团队和增长团队需要通力合作，或借鉴Salesforce的成功经验，因为在现阶段，开发者是不会接受销售人员强行推销的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you always come back to the psyche of the user and how in this case, developers like, here's why they're responsible for this thing. Salespeople are going to convince them this is going to work. And it's not. That's a really interesting tool and that's a really cool takeaway. (01:11:16): Is there anything else that we didn't cover before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你总能回归到用户的心理层面，比如在这种情况下，开发者会说"看，我们要对这件事负责"。销售人员会说服他们这项技术一定能成功。但事实并非如此。这是个非常有趣的工具，也是个很棒的收获。（01:11:16）：在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，还有什么我们没有讨论过的问题吗？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Plenty. I think we covered it all, man.
turns.zh: 有很多呢。我觉得我们已经把所有内容都覆盖到了，伙计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You got all my questions and more. So with that, welcome to the very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 你已经回答了我所有的问题，甚至更多了。那么，欢迎来到激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: I am so ready.
turns.zh: 我已经迫不及待了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: I'm a big believer in happiness. Not just being crunchy or we should all be happy, but also because it helps us do our best work and we're more creative and all this. So one is Simple Path to Wealth by JL Collins. I don't ignore the data, that money is something that often gets in the way of our happiness. I know so many smart people that just have not figured out the whole managing their finances thing. And this book will cover all of your basics. It's very easy to read. He's got an audiobook that he narrates himself. Simple Path to Wealth by JL Collins, he's fantastic.
turns.zh: 我非常推崇幸福的理念。不只是说要保持乐观，或者说我们都应该追求幸福，而是因为它能帮助我们发挥最佳水平，激发创造力等等。所以我推荐JL·柯林斯的《简单致富之道》。我不会忽视一个事实——金钱往往会阻碍我们获得幸福。我认识很多聪明人，他们就是没能搞清楚如何管理自己的财务。这本书会涵盖所有基础知识。读起来很轻松。他还有自己朗读的有声书。JL·柯林斯的《简单致富之道》，他太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a recent movie... Oh wait, wait, there's more?
turns.zh: 最近上映的电影……哦，等等，还有更多问题？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Oh, there's one more.
turns.zh: 哦，还有一个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, let's do it. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 好吧，那就开始吧。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: [inaudible 01:12:18] Happiness, which is Atomic Habits by James Clear. If you ever want to change something about yourself or something's not quite working for you, this guy will give you a framework to change it. Guaranteed.
turns.zh: [01:12:18不可听清]  关于幸福的，詹姆斯·克利尔的《原子习惯》。如果你想改变自己，或者某件事进展不顺利，这个人会给你一个改变的框架。保证有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really enjoyed that book. That guy's killing it. He was on Tim Ferris, he had a great interview. Folks that don't want to read it, they could listen to that. There's a lot of cool tips there. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢那本书。那个人太棒了。他上过蒂姆·费里斯的节目，采访很精彩。不想读这本书的人，可以去听听音频版。里面有很多实用建议。最近喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: Unabashedly, the Great British Baking Show. I love that show. I love that show for all the reasons everyone loves that show. It's heartwarming and makes you feel good and uplifts you. But also because it is a competitive show. They're trying to be the best baker and they're out there helping each other. They're like a big family. Most reality competitive TV shows that I see, all of them are like cutthroat, they're sabotaging. So I'm just endlessly fascinated also by the psychology of what's happening here. I want somebody to do a research paper on it, get to the bottom of why they're all helping each other. It's wonderful though. Wonderful to watch.
turns.zh: 毫不避讳地说，是《英国烘焙大赛》。我超爱那部剧。爱它是因为所有人爱它的原因——它温馨治愈，令人振奋。但更重要的是，它是一档竞技节目。他们努力成为最棒的烘焙师，同时互相帮助，就像一个大家庭。大多数真人竞技节目都是勾心斗角，互相拆台。所以我对这部剧的心理学层面也着迷不已。我希望有人能研究一下它，探究他们为什么能互相帮助。这部剧太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I always comes back to psychology with you.
turns.zh: 有意思。我跟你讨论心理学时总是会回归到这个层面。

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: I know. I know. I feel like I'm really, really sinking deep in there. And it's true though. It's very interesting to me, and I love that show.
turns.zh: 我知道。我知道。我感觉自己真的在深入探究这个领域。不过这确实很有趣，我也超爱那部剧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite interview question that you like to ask in interviews?
turns.zh: 你最喜欢在面试中问的一个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Laura Schaffer
turns.en: I love asking about a ship or release that is not cherry-picked by the person you're talking to. You can get it a lot of different ways. The thing is, everyone has a big success story. Everyone does. It really doesn't actually tell you very much to ask someone like, "What's a great thing you released?" Because everyone could tell that. Instead, take that away. What's the most recent ship is a really easy one because recency, time. But there's other things you can do to take that out. 我喜欢询问别人近期成功的案例，尤其是那些并非被对方刻意挑选出来的案例。你可以通过多种方式获取信息。但关键在于，每个人都有自己的成功故事。事实上，人们通常会把成功归功于某个特定项目或产品。这其实并不能真正传达出关键信息——比如问别人“你发布过的最棒的产品是什么？”这种问题往往会让对方感到无话可说。

相反，你可以反问他们：“最近推出的产品是什么？”这样既能避开对方刻意选择的案例，又能让对话更深入。毕竟，人们往往会更乐意分享近期成果，而非过往辉煌。通过这种方式，你能更清楚地了解他们的框架和方法论，而非单纯的结果。

因为如果你随意挑选某个案例，十有八九不是特别成功的。对方往往更愿意深入探讨他们的方法论和框架，而这正是你判断他们能否成功的关键所在。
